Three horses stand dozing at the hitching rail outside the general store, reins looped loose, tails flicking at flies in the afternoon heat.
A six-horse stagecoach rolls hard down the center of the street, trailing a long banner of red dust, passengers gripping the rail as it sways.
Two cowboys lean against a porch post outside the saloon, one gesturing with his hat, deep in some argument the street cannot hear.
A heavy ox-team hauls a loaded supply wagon through the mud ruts, the driver slapping the reins, sacks of grain stacked tall behind him.
A card game has moved to the saloon porch, four men hunched over a barrel table, a small stack of coins catching the midday light.
A lone rider walks his horse unhurried down the center of the street, the animal's hooves raising little puffs of dust with each slow step.
A herd of longhorns pushes through the main street in a rolling brown tide, two drovers riding the flanks shouting through the dust and bawling.
The blacksmith stands at his open forge, hammer raised mid-swing, orange sparks scattering across the dirt floor of the open-fronted shop.
Three women in long cotton dresses cross the street carrying wrapped parcels, stepping carefully around the deep wheel ruts left by the morning wagons.
A Native rider moves through the far end of the street at an easy walk, sitting straight and unhurried, the crowd parting without fuss around him.
A peddler's brightly painted wagon has stopped near the feed store, a small cluster of townsfolk pressing close to examine the goods laid out along its side.
A horse rears suddenly at the smell of smoke from the smithy, front hooves clawing the air while a man lunges for the trailing reins.
Two figures stand still at opposite ends of the block, twenty yards between them, neither moving, the street gone quiet around that narrow strip of dust.
A boy chases a runaway chicken between the legs of horses tied at the rail, the birds shrieking, the horses shifting and stamping with irritation.
The stagecoach driver climbs down stiffly from the box, handing the lines off to a waiting hostler while a small crowd gathers at the coach door.
A cowboy sits on the edge of the boardwalk, boots in the dust, turning his hat in his hands and watching the street with no particular hurry.
An old man on a mule picks through the far end of the herd, the cattle parting around him, dust rising to his stirrups in slow golden rolls.
Two drovers argue at the mouth of the livery, one pointing down the street, a third man leaning against the door frame listening without comment.
A woman hangs washing on a line strung between the back of her building and a fence post, the white sheets billowing into the dusty street wind.
The peddler stands on the wagon's folding step, holding up a brass-fitted case, a ranch hand in the crowd leaning in squinting to get a better look.
Four horses drink together at the long trough near the well, heads down and ears relaxed, their riders nowhere visible on the quiet afternoon street.
A rancher leads a skittish young horse through the middle of the street by a short rope, talking low to it while traffic parts on either side.
The blacksmith plunges a glowing horseshoe into the water barrel, a great hiss of white steam rising and drifting slowly across the open stable doors behind him.
A small dog bolts from beneath the boardwalk straight into the path of the incoming stagecoach, the lead horses veering slightly, the driver cursing from the box.
At the far end of the street the two figures still have not moved, dust drifting between them, a third man watching from a doorway with his arms folded.
